parts.title: The case of the missing cake
parts.instructions: Read the article and choose the best answer for each question.
parts.passage:
Last Saturday, my little cousin Tom and I became detectives. We were staying at our grandmother's house, and just before lunch, a big chocolate cake disappeared from the kitchen table. Grandma was very upset, because she had baked it for a party.

We started by looking for clues. On the floor, there were small brown footprints that led from the kitchen to the garden. "The thief has dirty shoes," Tom said, and wrote it in his notebook. There was also a little cream on the door handle.

We followed the footprints across the grass until they stopped under a big tree. There, we found the empty plate. Next to it was Max, our neighbour's dog, who was fast asleep with chocolate on his nose.

We took the plate back to Grandma, and she could not stop laughing. She said that she would bake another cake and keep it in the fridge. Tom wants to be a real detective now, and he has asked for a magnifying glass for his birthday.

options: A cake she had made was gone
questions.explanation: A big cake disappeared, and she had baked it for a party.

questions.prompt: What did the children find on the floor?
questions.explanation: There were small brown footprints.

options: To a tree in the garden
questions.explanation: They stopped under a big tree.
Max, the neighbour's dog, was asleep with chocolate on his nose.

questions.explanation: He has asked for a magnifying glass.

parts.title: The queen of crime
parts.instructions: Choose the sentence that fits each gap. There is one extra sentence.
parts.passage:
Agatha Christie is one of the most famous writers in the world. [1] Her books have been sold more than two billion times, and only the Bible and Shakespeare have sold more.

She was born in 1890 in the south of England. As a child, she did not go to school. [2] She learned to read when she was only five, and from then on she spent hours with books.

During the First World War, she worked in a hospital. [3] This knowledge later helped her to write about poisons in her stories.

Her first detective book appeared in 1920. [4] It introduced Hercule Poirot, a little Belgian detective with a famous moustache.

She wrote over eighty books in her life. [5] People still enjoy trying to guess who the criminal is before the end.
sentences: Her mother taught her at home, in a house full of books.
It was soon followed by many more cases for him to solve.
There, she learned a great deal about medicines.
Some of them have been made into films and television series.
She was already well known when she was still quite young.
No other writer of detective stories has been as successful as she has.

gaps.explanation: No other writer has been as successful; the next sentence gives sales.
Her mother taught her at home, which explains why she did not go to school.
There, she learned about medicines, which leads to poisons in her stories.
It was followed by many more cases for Poirot, introduced in the sentence before.
Some of them were made into films, and the next sentence says people still enjoy them.

parts.title: A message about a book
parts.instructions: Choose the correct word for each gap.
parts.passage: Hi Gaby, Have you finished the detective book that I lent you? I am dying to know [1] you think of it. I read it in two days, and I could not stop turning the pages. The ending was a big surprise, [2] I had guessed that the butler was the criminal. It is the first time that a book has [3] me wrong! If you have not read the last chapter, please do not tell me [4] I have finished it. I [5] already bought the next book in the series, and I will start it tonight. Perhaps we could meet on Saturday and talk about both books. I will bring some biscuits, [6] you can make the tea. Best, Gwen

questions.explanation: Know what you think of it: the object clause.
A surprise, although I had guessed: contrast.
Proved me wrong is the fixed phrase.
Do not tell me until I have finished it: a time limit.
I have already bought: present perfect.
I will bring biscuits and you can make the tea.

parts.title: How finger marks solve crimes
parts.instructions: Write one word in each gap.
parts.passage: Every person has a different pattern on the ends of their fingers. We call this a finger mark. Even twins do not have exactly [1] same finger marks. Detectives have used them to catch criminals for more than a hundred years. When somebody touches a glass or a door, they leave a tiny mark [2] oil from their skin. Police officers cover the mark with a fine powder, and then it becomes easy to see. They take a photograph of it and compare it [3] the prints of people who have been arrested before. Today, a computer can search millions of finger marks in a few seconds. Of course, a criminal who wears gloves will not leave any marks, [4] it is not always so easy to solve a case. Police also look for other clues, [5] as hair, clothes or blood. Together, all these small pieces of evidence help them to tell the true story of what happened [6] the crime scene.

gaps.explanation: The same finger marks: a fixed phrase.
A mark of oil from their skin.
A criminal who wears gloves leaves no marks, so it is not easy.
Such as hair or clothes: a fixed phrase.

parts.title: A talk about a famous detective
parts.instructions: Listen to the talk and complete each note with one word.

turns.speaker: nathalie
turns.text: Good afternoon, everybody. Today I would like to talk to you about Sherlock Holmes, the most famous detective in fiction. He was invented by a Scottish writer, Arthur Conan Doyle, who was also a doctor. The first story appeared in 1887, and Holmes became so popular that readers sent him letters, as if he were real. Holmes lived at 221B Baker Street in London, with his friend Doctor Watson. He played the violin, smoked a pipe and wore a long hat with ears. He did not use guns often. Instead, he used his brain, and he noticed tiny details that other people missed. Doyle wrote fifty-six short stories and four novels about him. Once, he got tired of the character and killed him in a story, but readers were so angry that he had to bring him back. If you would like to see where the stories take place, there is a museum at the address, and it is open every day from nine thirty.

gaps.prompt: Sherlock Holmes was invented by a ___ writer
gaps.explanation: He was invented by a Scottish writer.
He lived with his friend Doctor Watson.

gaps.prompt: The museum opens every day at ___
gaps.explanation: It is open every day from nine thirty.

parts.title: An interview with a police detective
parts.instructions: Listen to the interview and choose the correct answer.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: Gideon, you have been a detective for fifteen years. Is the job like it is on television?

turns.speaker: h
turns.text: Not at all. On television, cases are solved in one hour. In real life, they can take months, and most of the work is reading and talking.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: What skills do you need?

turns.speaker: h
turns.text: Patience and a good memory. You also have to listen carefully, because small details in people's stories often show the truth.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: What is the hardest part?

turns.speaker: h
turns.text: Speaking to the families of people who have been hurt. You must be calm and kind, even when it is very sad.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: Do you ever take your work home?

turns.speaker: h
turns.text: Sometimes. I cannot stop thinking about a case. My wife says I talk about it in my sleep!

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: What do you enjoy most?

turns.speaker: h
turns.text: The moment when all the pieces finally fit together. That feeling is worth all the long hours.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: What do you do to relax?

turns.speaker: h
turns.text: I do crossword puzzles and I walk in the hills with my dog. It clears my head.
